items.title: I can distinguish between a stressor and stress
items.what: A stressor is the stimulus (internal or external) that triggers the stress response. Stress is the psychological and physiological experience that results from encountering something that demands attention or coping effort.
items.why: Using these terms correctly is required in exam responses. Confusing them is a common error that costs marks, and precise language reflects accurate conceptual understanding.
items.example: An upcoming psychology exam is the stressor. The worry, increased heart rate, and difficulty sleeping that follow are the stress response.

subtopic.name: Stressors and Stress Responses
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the definition of stress and stressors, the distinction between internal and external stressors, psychological stress responses including eustress and distress, and the two key physiological stress responses: the flight-or-fight-or-freeze response in acute stress and the role of cortisol in chronic stress.
subtopic.why: Understanding how stressors are categorised and how the body and mind respond helps explain why different people experience stress differently and why certain physiological reactions occur. This foundational knowledge underpins all subsequent models studied in this topic.

items.title: I can distinguish between internal and external stressors and give examples of each
items.what: Internal stressors originate from within the person and include cognitive and biological factors such as negative attitude, rumination, low self-esteem, and nervous system dysfunction (e.g. low GABA). External stressors originate from the environment, such as exams, financial difficulty, or arguments with others.
items.why: This distinction is directly tested and helps explain why two people in the same situation can experience very different levels of stress. Internal stressors shape how external events are perceived.
items.example: A student sitting an exam (external stressor) repeatedly tells themselves they will fail (rumination, an internal stressor), amplifying their stress beyond what the exam alone would produce.

subtopic.why: Understanding how stressors are categorised and how the body and mind respond helps explain why different people experience stress differently and why certain physiological reactions occur. This foundational knowledge underpins all subsequent models studied in this topic.

items.title: I can explain the difference between eustress and distress as psychological stress responses
items.what: Eustress is a form of stress characterised by a positive psychological state, involving emotions such as excitement and motivation. Distress is a form of stress characterised by a negative psychological state, involving emotions such as worry and frustration. Both demonstrate the subjective nature of stress.
items.why: Recognising that stress is not always negative is important for understanding why the same stressor can produce different responses in different individuals. Eustress can actually enhance performance.
items.example: Two students are told they have been selected to represent the school at a debate. One feels motivated and excited (eustress); the other feels overwhelmed and dreads the event (distress).

subtopic.why: Understanding how stressors are categorised and how the body and mind respond helps explain why different people experience stress differently and why certain physiological reactions occur. This foundational knowledge underpins all subsequent models studied in this topic.

items.title: I can describe the flight-or-fight-or-freeze response as a physiological response to acute stress
items.what: Acute stress is intense and brief. The flight-or-fight-or-freeze response is an involuntary, automatic reaction to an immediate threat. Flight and fight involve sympathetic nervous system activation and adrenaline release. Freeze involves a brief parasympathetic activation causing immobility, followed by sympathetic activation.
items.why: This response explains why the body reacts so rapidly to immediate danger. Understanding the role of the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems in each component is required for exam questions.
items.example: A student is unexpectedly called on to answer a question in class. They may feel a surge of energy and speak up (fight), feel the urge to leave the room (flight), or go blank and be unable to respond (freeze).

subtopic.why: Understanding how stressors are categorised and how the body and mind respond helps explain why different people experience stress differently and why certain physiological reactions occur. This foundational knowledge underpins all subsequent models studied in this topic.

items.title: I can explain the role of cortisol in chronic stress
items.what: Chronic stress endures for several months or longer. Cortisol is a hormone released by the adrenal glands that helps maintain heightened arousal over this extended period. In the short term it increases blood sugar, improves metabolism, energises the body, and reduces inflammation. With prolonged elevation, cortisol suppresses the immune system.
items.why: Cortisol explains the biological mechanism behind long-term stress effects including increased susceptibility to illness. It also links lesson 3A content to Selye's GAS model studied in lesson 3B.
items.example: A student under exam pressure for an entire school year has sustained elevated cortisol. By late in the year they develop frequent colds as their immune system has been chronically suppressed.

subtopic.why: Understanding how stressors are categorised and how the body and mind respond helps explain why different people experience stress differently and why certain physiological reactions occur. This foundational knowledge underpins all subsequent models studied in this topic.

items.title: I can compare psychological and physiological stress responses
items.what: Psychological stress responses (eustress and distress) are subjective, varying between individuals experiencing the same stressor. Physiological stress responses (such as the fight-or-flight-or-freeze response and cortisol release) are largely objective, occurring in similar ways across different people.
items.why: This comparison is a recurring exam question type. Understanding the subjective versus objective distinction is essential for correctly applying these concepts to novel scenarios.
items.example: Two people watch the same horror film. Both experience increased heart rate (similar physiological response), but one finds it thrilling (eustress) while the other finds it deeply unsettling (distress).

items.title: I can describe the overall structure of Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome
items.what: Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) is a biological model involving three stages of physiological reactions in response to a persistent stressor: alarm reaction, resistance, and exhaustion. The alarm reaction stage has two substages: shock and counter shock.
items.why: Knowing the structure before the detail of each stage is required because exam questions often ask students to name stages in order, identify which stage a person is in, or write out the full name and acronym correctly on first use.
items.example: In an exam answer: 'Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) proposes that when Bob first encountered the stressor he entered the alarm reaction stage...'

subtopic.name: Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers Hans Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) as a biological model of stress with three stages: alarm reaction (shock and counter shock), resistance, and exhaustion. It also addresses the explanatory power of the model, including its strengths and limitations.
subtopic.why: The GAS is the key biological model of stress in the VCE study design. Understanding the distinct physiological characteristics of each stage, including the role of cortisol, allows students to apply the model to scenarios and evaluate it critically.

items.title: I can describe the shock and counter shock substages of the alarm reaction
items.what: Shock is the first substage in which bodily arousal briefly drops below normal following initial exposure to a stressor: body temperature, blood pressure, and muscle tone temporarily decrease. Counter shock follows immediately, with sympathetic nervous system activation causing adrenaline and cortisol release, raising arousal above normal.
items.why: Exam questions often present a scenario and ask students to identify both the stage and the substage. Identifying alarm reaction without specifying the substage is insufficient for full marks.
items.example: Sophie crashes her car. Immediately after impact she freezes and cannot think clearly (shock). Seconds later her heart pounds, she feels a rush of adrenaline, and she is able to exit the vehicle and exchange details (counter shock).

subtopic.name: Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers Hans Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) as a biological model of stress with three stages: alarm reaction (shock and counter shock), resistance, and exhaustion. It also addresses the explanatory power of the model, including its strengths and limitations.
subtopic.why: The GAS is the key biological model of stress in the VCE study design. Understanding the distinct physiological characteristics of each stage, including the role of cortisol, allows students to apply the model to scenarios and evaluate it critically.

items.title: I can describe the resistance stage of the GAS
items.what: In the resistance stage, bodily arousal remains above normal as the body adjusts to and maintains a heightened physiological state. Elevated cortisol sustains this arousal. The body directs most of its resources toward the initial stressor, reducing resistance to additional stressors. Mild illness may develop due to beginning immune suppression.
items.why: Resistance is commonly confused with exhaustion in exam responses. The key distinction is that in resistance the person can still cope with the demands of the stressor despite showing early signs of stress-related illness.
items.example: A student facing ongoing study pressure develops occasional headaches and catches a cold, but continues to attend school, study, and meet deadlines. This indicates resistance, not exhaustion.

subtopic.name: Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers Hans Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) as a biological model of stress with three stages: alarm reaction (shock and counter shock), resistance, and exhaustion. It also addresses the explanatory power of the model, including its strengths and limitations.
subtopic.why: The GAS is the key biological model of stress in the VCE study design. Understanding the distinct physiological characteristics of each stage, including the role of cortisol, allows students to apply the model to scenarios and evaluate it critically.

items.title: I can describe the exhaustion stage of the GAS
items.what: In exhaustion, bodily resources including energy and stress hormones are depleted after prolonged exposure to the stressor. Arousal drops below normal, the person can no longer cope with the stressor, and immune suppression is severe. Serious physiological and psychological illness may develop, including cardiovascular disease, extreme fatigue, anxiety, and depression.
items.why: Distinguishing exhaustion from resistance requires understanding that exhaustion involves an inability to cope and serious illness, not merely mild symptoms. This distinction is directly tested using scenario-based questions.
items.example: After months of sustained financial and workplace stress, a person is diagnosed with a heart condition, is unable to go to work, and feels completely unable to manage daily demands. This indicates exhaustion.

subtopic.name: Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers Hans Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) as a biological model of stress with three stages: alarm reaction (shock and counter shock), resistance, and exhaustion. It also addresses the explanatory power of the model, including its strengths and limitations.
subtopic.why: The GAS is the key biological model of stress in the VCE study design. Understanding the distinct physiological characteristics of each stage, including the role of cortisol, allows students to apply the model to scenarios and evaluate it critically.

items.title: I can explain the role of cortisol across the stages of the GAS
items.what: Cortisol is released during counter shock to energise the body. Its sustained presence during resistance maintains heightened arousal but begins suppressing immune functioning. By exhaustion, cortisol and other stress hormones are depleted, contributing to the collapse of the body's ability to respond.
items.why: Cortisol links the GAS to the physiological content from lesson 3A and appears in multiple exam questions asking students to identify its role at a specific stage.
items.example: During resistance, Winnie's sustained cortisol levels keep her functioning under exam pressure but result in recurring viral infections as her immune system is suppressed.

subtopic.why: The GAS is the key biological model of stress in the VCE study design. Understanding the distinct physiological characteristics of each stage, including the role of cortisol, allows students to apply the model to scenarios and evaluate it critically.

items.title: I can evaluate the explanatory power of Selye's GAS by identifying its strengths and limitations
items.what: Strengths: the GAS identifies a measurable, predictable pattern of physiological responses and recognises the link between chronic stress and illness. Limitations: the model was based on rat studies (reducing generalisability to humans), ignores psychological factors such as cognition and emotion, and applies a uniform model to all individuals, failing to account for individual differences in stress responses.
items.why: Evaluating the GAS is explicitly required by the study design and directly assessed in exam questions. Understanding that a biological model's strength is also its limitation relative to a psychological model is a key insight.
items.example: A strength: the GAS correctly predicts that a person under prolonged stress will develop immune suppression. A limitation: it cannot explain why two people facing the same stressor for the same duration may progress through the stages at different rates.

items.title: I can explain what makes Lazarus and Folkman's model a psychological and transactional model of stress
items.what: The model is psychological because it focuses on subjective cognitive and affective appraisals of stressors rather than biological responses. It is transactional because stress is the output resulting from a transaction between an incoming stressor and the individual's personal appraisal of it and their available coping resources.
items.why: Understanding why this model is described as psychological and transactional is required for comparison questions with Selye's GAS and for correctly framing exam answers.
items.example: Two students receive the same exam result. One appraises it as a threat to their future (producing distress), while another appraises it as a challenge to improve (producing eustress). The stress that results is a product of this subjective transaction, not the result alone.

subtopic.name: Lazarus and Folkman's Transactional Model
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers Lazarus and Folkman's Transactional Model of Stress and Coping as a psychological model of stress, focusing on primary appraisal (including benign-positive, irrelevant, and stressful appraisals with harm/loss, threat, and challenge sub-appraisals) and secondary appraisal (including emotion-focused and problem-focused coping strategies). It also covers the model's strengths and limitations.
subtopic.why: This is the key psychological model of stress in the study design and provides the counterpart to Selye's biological model. Understanding it allows students to explain individual differences in stress responses and apply both models to the same scenario.

items.title: I can describe the first substage of primary appraisal, including the three possible initial appraisals
items.what: In the first substage of primary appraisal, the individual evaluates whether an incoming stimulus will cause them stress. The three possible appraisals are: irrelevant (not an issue for the individual), benign-positive (neutral or good, not stressful), or stressful (a source of worry or emotional significance). Only a stressful appraisal continues the transaction.
items.why: Students must know all three initial appraisals and understand that the model only progresses if the stimulus is judged stressful. This is frequently tested using novel scenarios.
items.example: A student hears that a new elective subject has been added to the school timetable. They appraise it as irrelevant because it does not affect them. No further appraisal occurs and no stress results.

subtopic.name: Lazarus and Folkman's Transactional Model
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers Lazarus and Folkman's Transactional Model of Stress and Coping as a psychological model of stress, focusing on primary appraisal (including benign-positive, irrelevant, and stressful appraisals with harm/loss, threat, and challenge sub-appraisals) and secondary appraisal (including emotion-focused and problem-focused coping strategies). It also covers the model's strengths and limitations.
subtopic.why: This is the key psychological model of stress in the study design and provides the counterpart to Selye's biological model. Understanding it allows students to explain individual differences in stress responses and apply both models to the same scenario.

items.title: I can describe the second substage of primary appraisal, including harm/loss, threat, and challenge
items.what: If the stimulus is appraised as stressful, the individual further categorises the nature of that stress: harm/loss means the stressor has already caused damage; threat means the stressor may cause damage in the future; challenge means the stressor may offer a positive opportunity for growth or change.
items.why: All three sub-appraisals produce different emotional responses and lead to different coping behaviours in secondary appraisal. Exam questions regularly ask students to identify which sub-appraisal applies to a given scenario and justify their answer.
items.example: Thomas is anxious about learning to drive. He appraises it as a threat because he fears future accidents and financial strain, not because anything bad has happened yet.

items.title: I can describe secondary appraisal and the two types of coping strategies it involves
items.what: Secondary appraisal is the evaluation of what coping resources are required and whether they are available. If coping resources are judged adequate, stress is reduced or eliminated. If inadequate, stress continues. Two coping strategies are identified: problem-focused coping (directly targeting the source of the stressor) and emotion-focused coping (targeting the emotional components of the stressor indirectly).
items.why: Secondary appraisal explains why two people who make the same primary appraisal of a stressor can still end up with different stress levels. It is also directly linked to the coping strategies content in lesson 3E.
items.example: Yasmin appraises running out of savings as a threat (primary appraisal) and then evaluates whether she has enough time and income opportunities to rebuild them (secondary appraisal). Concluding she does not, her stress increases.

subtopic.name: Lazarus and Folkman's Transactional Model
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers Lazarus and Folkman's Transactional Model of Stress and Coping as a psychological model of stress, focusing on primary appraisal (including benign-positive, irrelevant, and stressful appraisals with harm/loss, threat, and challenge sub-appraisals) and secondary appraisal (including emotion-focused and problem-focused coping strategies). It also covers the model's strengths and limitations.
subtopic.why: This is the key psychological model of stress in the study design and provides the counterpart to Selye's biological model. Understanding it allows students to explain individual differences in stress responses and apply both models to the same scenario.

items.title: I can give examples of problem-focused and emotion-focused coping strategies
items.what: Problem-focused strategies directly address the source of the stressor: making a plan, seeking information, taking action, time management. Emotion-focused strategies address the emotional experience of the stressor indirectly: wishful thinking, denial, reframing, venting, meditation, distraction.
items.why: Students must be able to identify and apply both types of coping strategy to novel scenarios. Neither type is inherently superior; effectiveness depends on the specific context of the stressor.
items.example: A student stressed about an upcoming SAC uses problem-focused coping by making a study timetable, and emotion-focused coping by calling a friend to vent before returning to study.

It also covers the model's strengths and limitations.
subtopic.why: This is the key psychological model of stress in the study design and provides the counterpart to Selye's biological model. Understanding it allows students to explain individual differences in stress responses and apply both models to the same scenario.

items.title: I can evaluate the explanatory power of Lazarus and Folkman's model by identifying its strengths and limitations
items.what: Strengths: the model accounts for individual differences in stress responses, uses human subjects, incorporates cognitive processes, and provides coping strategies. Limitations: primary and secondary appraisal may occur simultaneously rather than in sequence, individuals are not always consciously aware of their appraisals, and the model lacks empirical support because internal appraisal processes are difficult to test.
items.why: Evaluating both models and comparing them is explicitly required by the study design. What is typically a strength of the Lazarus and Folkman model is often a limitation of Selye's GAS, and vice versa.
items.example: A strength: the model explains why Dean is less stressed than Yasmin after the same trip, because their appraisals differ. A limitation: neither Dean nor Yasmin may be consciously aware of the appraisal steps the model describes.

items.title: I can define the gut and distinguish between gut microbiota and the gut microbiome
items.what: The gut (gastrointestinal tract) is the tube from mouth to anus responsible for digestion. Gut microbiota refers to all the microorganisms (bacteria, fungi, viruses) that live in the gut. The gut microbiome refers to all the genes of those microorganisms. A diverse microbiota with more 'good' bacteria is associated with better gut health.
items.why: These terms are distinct and both appear in exam questions. Confusing microbiota with microbiome is a common error. Understanding what constitutes a healthy microbiota is the foundation for understanding how gut health relates to psychological processes.
items.example: If a student's gut has many different species of beneficial bacteria (diverse microbiota), this is associated with better overall health outcomes, including lower levels of stress.

subtopic.name: The Gut-Brain Axis
subtopic.what: This subtopic introduces the gut and gut microbiota, defines the gut-brain axis as a bidirectional connection between the gut and the brain via the enteric and central nervous systems, and examines emerging research linking gut microbiota composition to stress, mental illness, and behaviour.
subtopic.why: The gut-brain axis is an explicitly listed area of emerging research in the study design. Students must understand the mechanism of bidirectional communication, the role of gut microbiota, and the nature and limitations of the evidence — including why definitive causal claims cannot yet be made.

items.title: I can define the gut-brain axis and explain what makes it bidirectional
items.what: The gut-brain axis is the bidirectional connection between the gut and the brain through the enteric nervous system and the central nervous system. Bidirectional means communication flows both ways: the gut influences the brain and the brain influences the gut. The vagus nerve is the primary physical pathway for this communication, with approximately 80-90% of its fibres carrying signals from gut to brain.
items.why: The bidirectional nature of the relationship is central to understanding how stress affects the gut and how gut health affects stress. Exam questions may ask students to explain or give examples of communication in both directions.
items.example: When a student feels anxious before an exam (brain to gut), they may experience stomach cramps. Conversely, a student with irritable bowel syndrome (gut to brain) may experience heightened anxiety as a result.

subtopic.name: The Gut-Brain Axis
subtopic.what: This subtopic introduces the gut and gut microbiota, defines the gut-brain axis as a bidirectional connection between the gut and the brain via the enteric and central nervous systems, and examines emerging research linking gut microbiota composition to stress, mental illness, and behaviour.
subtopic.why: The gut-brain axis is an explicitly listed area of emerging research in the study design. Students must understand the mechanism of bidirectional communication, the role of gut microbiota, and the nature and limitations of the evidence — including why definitive causal claims cannot yet be made.

items.title: I can describe the role of the enteric nervous system in the gut-brain axis
items.what: The enteric nervous system is the network of nerves in the gut and is a subdivision of the autonomic nervous system. It communicates with the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord), allowing gut-related conditions to influence brain function and brain-related conditions to influence gut function.
items.why: Students must be able to correctly locate the enteric nervous system within the broader nervous system hierarchy and explain its role in the gut-brain relationship, as this is likely to be assessed directly.
items.example: A person with inflammatory bowel disease (a gut condition) has altered enteric nervous system signals being sent to the brain, which can contribute to symptoms of anxiety or depression.

subtopic.name: The Gut-Brain Axis
subtopic.what: This subtopic introduces the gut and gut microbiota, defines the gut-brain axis as a bidirectional connection between the gut and the brain via the enteric and central nervous systems, and examines emerging research linking gut microbiota composition to stress, mental illness, and behaviour.
subtopic.why: The gut-brain axis is an explicitly listed area of emerging research in the study design. Students must understand the mechanism of bidirectional communication, the role of gut microbiota, and the nature and limitations of the evidence — including why definitive causal claims cannot yet be made.

items.title: I can describe emerging research evidence for the gut-brain axis, including germ-free animal studies and microbiota composition research
items.what: Germ-free animal studies remove gut microorganisms from animals and compare their behaviour to conventional animals. Findings include increased anxiety-like behaviour, poorer memory, increased stress hormones, and less social interaction in germ-free mice. Human studies compare microbiota composition in people with and without mental health conditions and suggest links between gut microbiota and stress, depression, anxiety, autism spectrum disorder, and cognitive decline.
items.why: The study design specifically requires reference to emerging research. Students must be able to describe findings without overstating them as proven causal relationships, which reflects appropriate scientific literacy.
items.example: In one study, germ-free mice implanted with gut microbiota from humans with major depressive disorder began exhibiting depressive-like behaviours, suggesting a possible link between gut microbiota composition and mood.

subtopic.name: The Gut-Brain Axis
subtopic.what: This subtopic introduces the gut and gut microbiota, defines the gut-brain axis as a bidirectional connection between the gut and the brain via the enteric and central nervous systems, and examines emerging research linking gut microbiota composition to stress, mental illness, and behaviour.
subtopic.why: The gut-brain axis is an explicitly listed area of emerging research in the study design. Students must understand the mechanism of bidirectional communication, the role of gut microbiota, and the nature and limitations of the evidence — including why definitive causal claims cannot yet be made.

items.title: I can explain the relationship between gut microbiota and stress, using the bidirectional nature of the gut-brain axis
items.what: The relationship between gut microbiota and stress is bidirectional. Experiencing stress can negatively affect the diversity and composition of gut microbiota. Conversely, having an unhealthy gut microbiota is linked to higher stress levels. This explains phenomena such as experiencing stomach discomfort when stressed and experiencing stress when suffering digestive problems.
items.why: This bidirectional relationship directly links gut-brain axis content to the broader topic of stress. Exam questions may present a scenario involving stress and gut symptoms and ask students to explain the connection.
items.example: A student who is chronically stressed about exams develops digestive discomfort (stress affecting the gut). Separately, a student with a gut condition may find their anxiety worsens when their gut symptoms flare (gut affecting stress levels).

subtopic.what: This subtopic introduces the gut and gut microbiota, defines the gut-brain axis as a bidirectional connection between the gut and the brain via the enteric and central nervous systems, and examines emerging research linking gut microbiota composition to stress, mental illness, and behaviour.
subtopic.why: The gut-brain axis is an explicitly listed area of emerging research in the study design. Students must understand the mechanism of bidirectional communication, the role of gut microbiota, and the nature and limitations of the evidence — including why definitive causal claims cannot yet be made.

items.title: I can explain why definitive conclusions about the gut-brain axis cannot yet be drawn
items.what: Because the gut-brain axis is an emerging area of research, findings are still evolving and sometimes contradictory. It is incorrect to state that gut microbiota causes stress or mental illness; rather, emerging research suggests possible connections. Animal studies are difficult to generalise to humans, and some studies using different strains of animals have produced conflicting results.
items.why: Scientific literacy requires understanding the difference between correlation and causation and between emerging findings and established consensus. This is explicitly acknowledged in the curriculum content and reflects the nature of this research area.
items.example: One study found less social engagement in germ-free mice; another study using a different strain of mice found normal social engagement. This contradiction shows the field is still developing and definitive conclusions are premature.

items.title: I can define and apply the concept of context-specific effectiveness
items.what: Context-specific effectiveness refers to selecting a coping strategy that is appropriate for the unique demands of the stressor, taking into account individual circumstances, available resources, the environment, and timing. The same strategy is not equally effective in all situations or for all people.
items.why: Exam questions frequently ask students to evaluate whether a coping strategy is context-specifically effective in a given scenario. This requires analysing specific details of the scenario rather than making general claims.
items.example: A student who has not yet studied for an upcoming SAC needs approach strategies such as creating a study timetable and seeking teacher help. The same strategies would be less urgent for a student who has already studied the content thoroughly.

subtopic.name: Coping with Stress
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the concepts of context-specific effectiveness and coping flexibility as components of effective stress management, and the two main categories of coping strategies: approach strategies (which directly confront the source of stress) and avoidance strategies (which evade the stressor to manage emotional components indirectly).
subtopic.why: Effective coping is directly linked to mental wellbeing and is assessed both as standalone content and in combination with Lazarus and Folkman's model. Students must be able to identify, apply, and evaluate coping strategies in novel and complex scenarios.

items.title: I can define and apply the concept of coping flexibility
items.what: Coping flexibility is the ability to adjust or change coping strategies when circumstances change, when the initial stressor evolves, or when the original strategy is no longer providing relief. High coping flexibility supports both context-specific effectiveness and overall mental wellbeing.
items.why: Coping flexibility is a distinct concept from context-specific effectiveness and is directly assessed. Students must be able to describe what it is and identify it in scenarios where a person changes their approach in response to changing demands.
items.example: A student normally relieves stress by playing football, but when the football season ends they switch to daily jogging instead. Adapting their coping strategy to the changed circumstances demonstrates coping flexibility.

subtopic.name: Coping with Stress
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the concepts of context-specific effectiveness and coping flexibility as components of effective stress management, and the two main categories of coping strategies: approach strategies (which directly confront the source of stress) and avoidance strategies (which evade the stressor to manage emotional components indirectly).
subtopic.why: Effective coping is directly linked to mental wellbeing and is assessed both as standalone content and in combination with Lazarus and Folkman's model. Students must be able to identify, apply, and evaluate coping strategies in novel and complex scenarios.

items.title: I can describe approach strategies and give examples
items.what: Approach strategies are coping strategies that directly confront the source of stress in order to reduce or eliminate it. They deal with stress in a practical way by targeting the stressor itself rather than the emotions associated with it. Examples include making a plan and executing it, seeking professional advice and implementing strategies, and making a list of ways to address the stressful situation.
items.why: Students must be able to correctly identify approach strategies in novel scenarios and distinguish them from avoidance strategies. Misidentifying one as the other is a common exam error.
items.example: Naima has fallen behind in schoolwork while caring for her injured mother. She creates a homework schedule and asks her teacher for an extension on an assignment. Both are approach strategies because they directly target the source of stress.

items.title: I can describe avoidance strategies and give examples
items.what: Avoidance strategies are coping strategies that evade or distance the person from the stressor, dealing with its emotional components indirectly rather than confronting its source. Examples include distraction, venting emotions, wishful thinking, denial, re-evaluation, sleeping, and eating.
items.why: Avoidance strategies are not inherently less effective than approach strategies. Their appropriateness depends on context. Students must avoid the misconception that avoidance is always unhelpful and apply contextual reasoning in their evaluations.
items.example: Dom has no idea what to say in his speech two days out, so he takes his dog for a walk and works on other things instead. This is an avoidance strategy: he is not directly addressing the speech, but the mental break allows an idea to emerge.

items.title: I can evaluate which coping strategy is most appropriate given a specific context
items.what: The effectiveness of approach versus avoidance strategies depends on the nature and controllability of the stressor, the individual's resources, and the stage of the stressor. For controllable stressors, approach strategies are often more effective. For stressors with limited controllability or during acute emotional distress, avoidance strategies may be more appropriate temporarily.
items.why: Evaluation of coping strategies in context is a high-level skill required for extended response questions. Students must go beyond simply labelling a strategy and instead justify whether it is effective given the specific circumstances presented.
items.example: Andrea's best friend of 50 years has died. Staying in bed and grieving (avoidance) is contextually appropriate given the traumatic, uncontrollable nature of the stressor. Demanding she immediately use approach strategies would not reflect context-specific effectiveness.

items.title: I can explain how coping flexibility and context-specific effectiveness work together to support mental wellbeing
items.what: Coping flexibility enables context-specific effectiveness by allowing a person to recognise when a current strategy is no longer working and to select a more appropriate one. Together, these capacities reduce the sustained impact of stressors and support an individual's mental wellbeing, defined as their ability to think, process information, and regulate emotions effectively.
items.why: Exam questions often present multi-part scenarios requiring students to identify both concepts and explain the relationship between them. Understanding that coping flexibility is the mechanism that produces context-specific effectiveness is a key conceptual link.
items.example: Ngoza ran to cope with SAC stress but after three SACs it was no longer reducing her anxiety. To demonstrate coping flexibility she would need to recognise this and trial a different strategy, such as study groups or mindfulness, to restore context-specific effectiveness.
